cur:monumental2-saqqara-virgin-nursing.summary: Within a painted niche crowned by an arch of medallion busts, the Virgin sits enthroned and turns slightly as she offers her breast to the Christ Child, who leans in from the left, gripping her with both hands. The tender, unusual subject of the nursing Mother of God – the Galaktotrophousa – appears here in one of its earliest monumental examples.
facts: The photograph comes from J. E. Quibell's excavation report, Excavations at Saqqara (1908–9, 1909–10): The Monastery of Apa Jeremias, published in 1912.

The Egyptian image of the nursing Virgin is often compared with earlier Egyptian depictions of Isis nursing Horus, though the Christian image carries its own theological meaning: the true humanity of the Son of God.

cur:monumental2-saqqara-virgin-nursing.notes: Present location not verified from a museum record (the main Saqqara wall paintings were transferred to the Coptic Museum, Cairo). Dating of the Saqqara cell paintings varies between the 6th and 8th centuries.

cur:objects-princeton-nikephoros-group-c.summary: Christ hangs on the cross between the sun and moon, his body slightly swaying, with the Virgin standing at the left and St John at the right holding a book. The figures are carved with broad, simple forms and stand on a narrow ground line beneath the cross. The plaque belongs to a group of ivories whose sober, monumental style is associated with the reign of Nikephoros II Phokas.
facts: The museum attributes it to the 'Nikephoros Group', a set of ivories named after the ivory staurotheke (cross reliquary) at Cortona, which bears the name of the emperor Nikephoros II Phokas (963–969).

Q29385370.summary: Under a lacy openwork canopy, Christ hangs in death on the cross, his body slumped and clothed only in a loincloth, while the Virgin gestures toward him and Saint John raises a hand to his face in grief. Below the footrest three soldiers cast lots for the seamless robe, and at the very bottom the foot of the cross pierces the belly of a reclining bearded figure, Hades, ruler of the dead. Large areas of plain ivory make a quiet stage for this image of Christ's victory over death.
facts: The Met describes the motif of the cross planted in the stomach of Hades as a unique detail; an inscription on the ivory reads 'the cross implanted in the stomach of Hades'.
It is the only surviving part of a triptych whose wings are lost, and was probably used for private devotion.
The Met compares its gentle, introspective mood to the 11th-century Crucifixion mosaic at the Monastery of Daphni near Athens.
